To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the robotic navigation system requires significantly increased operative times while providing no significant advantages over the imageless CAS system with regard to predicting the postopera tive acetabular component alignment.

there was no significant difference in the accuracy of the robotic system versus the imageless, computer assisted navigation system in predicting the post operative acetabular position, and that there was a significant difference in operative times.

1) there was a statistically significant difference between the two groups for operative times, 2) there was no significant difference between the robotic and CAS groups with regards to the accuracy of predicting the postoperative alignment, 3) all acetabular components in both groups were within the safe zone for both abduction and anteversion as defined by Lewinnek, and 4) the interobserver correlation coefficients were high for both the robotic and CAS cohorts.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MAKO(tm)-robotic navigation system does not appear to be superior to the imageless, AchieveCAS system in predicting the postoperatively position of the acetabulum in total hip arthrophasties.

the MAKO(tm)-robotic navigation system does not provide a significant advantage over the AchieveCAS system with respect to the accuracy of the intraoperative readings in predicting the post-operative component position.
the imageless, computer assisted system is a more efficient method for achieving accurate component alignment, and is therefore a better choice for routine THA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the imageless, Achieve CAS system is an excellent tool for predicting the final post-operative acetabular position.
the MAKO robotic arm assisted navigation system does not provide any advantage over the image less computer assisted surgery system.
the robotic navigation system is not superior to the CAS system in predicting postoperative acetabulum position.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the robotic navigation system is not a necessary component of a CAS system.
, in our experience, the robotic navigation system is not superior to an imageless, computer assisted system in predicting the post operative acetabular component alignment in THA.
the MAKO(tm robotic navigation system is no better than the AchieveCAS system in predicting the postop component position.
